So mobile plans are starting to look like a net neutrality proponent's worst nightmare, T-Mobile for example gives unlimited data for some very bandwidth intensive services (e.g. Youtube, Pandora, Netflix, Spotify) but you generally only get a few gigs for everything else unless you pay a lot extra for more data. So if you prefer another service not covered, like say you use Hulu to stream and your mobile provider doesn't make their data free than it's unusable on mobile. Also some niche services such as fetish porn sites with user generated content would be hit harder.

Bonus question: are there any mobile providers that give you unlimited data with tethering at a reasonable price?
Should mobile data caps be banned or regulated?

IMO data caps should be allowed as long as they are clearly communicated to the customer. But flat rate plans should be flat rate plans. If someone wants fast internet but doesn't need much capacity, fine give them a cheaper contract which slows after the limit is reached. But users who pay for normal service shouldn't be capped.
Are there providers which offer a plan with no caps, throttling, or limits on tethering?
I don't know, depends on where you are.
I have a Sprint plan with unlimited everything for $70/mo. Not sure if they throttle. Unlimited tethering with rooted os

Well, it depends. Honesty is the first requirement. If you're offering full data for a flat rate, no extras, then it needs to be just that, no quibbling. If you don't, then say so.

That said, companies also need to be held to the truth about what data costs them. If Google can offer what it does and make money, then so can ComCast, so can Cox, etc.

Bandwidth usage goes up every day. On wi-fi, for example, I regularly stream bunches of YouTube videos as well as watch TV. I don't mind paying, but it has to be equitable.

So. I guess I'm for regulation, as long as it actually provides a fair deal for all concerned. Unfortunately, the utility providers usually don't, and that does need to change.

It should be supported rather soon, but don't expect it to work with 14.04. It'll require a much more recent kernel than what that distro provides. I do expect 16.10 to support it.

There's very little reason to use LTS on a desktop at home. LTS is good for enterprises who want to have stable software, and by stable I mean that they don't change much.

I'd rather have LTS than have my shit break randomly while updating in a Rolling, or having to deal with 6 months of extended beta testing in a period release. 14.04 is stable, and old, and that’s NOT a bad thing in most cases.

Well, you are free to use what you want. Debian wouldn't exist if nobody saw the value of long term releases. On the other hand, Linux moves really fast, especially compared to the other mainstream OSes, that you are limiting yourself (IMO, in my experience).

I personally use a rolling release because I want the new stuff NOW and I'm willing to sacrifice the stability of my system for that. One thing I realized is that the instability seems to come from a few distinct groups. GNOME was a big one, systemd is another (and those two work together, being RedHat projects). Once I got rid of GNOME, updates became way safer.
